claim: NFPA 72 requires an emergency communication system to achieve an STI of at least 0.45 at 90% of measurement locations within each acoustically distinguishable space, with an average STI of at least 0.50 across the space.
source_title: Mass Notification: Intelligibility is NOT Optional
supporting_excerpt: voice intelligibility ... is considered acceptable if at least 90 percent of the measurement locations within each acoustically distinguishable space (ADS) have a measured STI of not less than 0.45 (0.65 CIS) and an average STI of not less than 0.50 (0.70 CIS).
airport_or_entity: US code framework applicable to MWAA
denominator: measurement locations per acoustically distinguishable space
caveat: Secondary source; primary text is NFPA 72 Chapter 24 and Annex D, which are paywalled.

claim: NFPA 72 Chapter 24 defines Emergency Communication Systems and requires that they be capable of reproducing prerecorded, synthesized, or live messages with voice intelligibility per Chapter 18.
source_title: Chapter 24, Emergency Communication Systems (ECS) of NFPA 72 (Honeywell white paper)
supporting_excerpt: Emergency communications systems shall be capable of the reproduction of prerecorded, synthesized, or live messages with voice intelligibility in accordance with Chapter 18.
airport_or_entity: US code framework applicable to MWAA
caveat: Vendor white paper; primary source is NFPA 72, Chapter 24, which is paywalled.

claim: ACRP Research Report 175 recommends a minimum STI of 0.45 and a signal-to-noise ratio of 10-15 dB for public address announcements in airport departure lounges.
source_title: Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems (ACRP Research Report 175), Chapter 3
supporting_excerpt: recommends maintaining an SNR of 10 dB(A) and a minimum STI of 0.45 for public address broadcasts in pier-style departure lounges
denominator: measurement points within pier-style departure lounge ADS
caveat: Guidance document; not binding without adoption in a design manual or code overlay.

claim: Many existing large, distributed sound systems in airports are in poor condition for intelligibility purposes and require significant calibration before intelligibility can even be measured.
source_title: Voice Intelligibility in Mass Notification Systems (Suppression Systems, summarizing ACRP 175 and Chapter 24 practice)
supporting_excerpt: Existing large, distributed sound systems in airports are often in poor condition for intelligibility purposes, requiring significant calibration work before intelligibility measurements can be properly collected.

claim: 14 CFR 139.319 requires that within 3 minutes of alarm, at least one required ARFF vehicle reach the midpoint of the farthest runway serving air carrier aircraft (or a comparable point on the movement area) and begin application of extinguishing agent; other required vehicles must reach that point within 4 minutes.
source_title: 14 CFR 139.319 - Aircraft rescue and firefighting: Operational requirements
supporting_excerpt: Within 3 minutes from the time of the alarm, at least one required aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicle must reach the midpoint of the farthest runway serving air carrier aircraft ... and begin application of extinguishing agent.
airport_or_entity: US Part 139 airports including IAD and DCA
caveat: Response clock starts at alarm; terminal-side alarm and dispatch latency are inputs.

claim: 49 CFR Part 1542 requires each airport operator to provide law enforcement personnel adequate to support its security program, including uniformed LEOs adequate to support screening operations under Parts 1544/1546.
source_title: 49 CFR Part 1542 - Airport Security
page_or_section: Subpart C - Operations, law enforcement provisions
supporting_excerpt: each airport operator required to have a security program must provide law enforcement personnel in the number and manner adequate to support its security program, including uniformed law enforcement personnel adequate to support each system for screening persons and accessible property required under part 1544 or 1546
airport_or_entity: US commercial-service airports including IAD and DCA
caveat: Specific LEO response-time floors are contained in SSI-protected Airport Security Programs and not in the public regulation.

claim: MWAA Police Department officers enforce Airports Authority regulations, the county codes of Arlington, Fairfax, and Loudoun Counties, and the laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia, with jurisdiction across terminals, airport property and roadways, and the Dulles Toll Road and Dulles Access Highway.
source_title: MWAA Police Department
supporting_excerpt: MWAA police officers enforce Airports Authority regulations, the county codes of Arlington, Fairfax, and Loudoun Counties, and the laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Their jurisdiction includes the Airport terminals, Airport property and roadways which includes the miles of highway that comprise the Dulles Toll Road and Dulles Access Highway.
caveat: MWAA-authored description; scope of concurrent jurisdiction with host counties not fully detailed on this page.

claim: The MWAA Fire and Rescue Department was formed from the FAA's ARFF branch when MWAA was established in 1987 and today comprises approximately 163 personnel: 16 chief officers, 27 fire officers, 21 master firefighters, 90 firefighters, and 9 civilian staff.
source_title: Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority Fire and Rescue Department
supporting_excerpt: The department is comprised of 163 personnel, consisting of 16 chief officers, 27 fire officers, 21 master firefighters, 90 firefighters and 9 civilian staff.
data_vintage: as of the article's most recent update
caveat: Secondary source; MWAA should be asked for current authorized strength and vacancy rate.

claim: SFO's Quiet Airport program removed more than 90 minutes of daily announcement time and reduced onsite noise by more than 40%, retained automated safety and security messaging as an explicit carveout, and delivered the reduction primarily through zoned paging and script discipline.
source_title: Inside San Francisco Airport's 'Quiet Airport' Initiative
supporting_excerpt: removed over 90 minutes' worth of unnecessary daily noise ... reduced overall onsite noise by more than 40% ... banned all automatic announcements apart from those related to safety and security
units: minutes/day of announcement time; percentage reduction in onsite noise
caveat: Airport-reported metrics; underlying measurement methodology not publicly documented.

claim: On January 6, 2017, the FLL primary shooting event began at approximately 12:54 PM with radio calls of shots fired from Broward Sheriff's Office deputies and multiple 911 callers, and Regional Communications immediately activated Active Shooter/Mass Casualty protocols.
source_title: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport Active Shooter Incident and Post-Event Response After Action Report
supporting_excerpt: At 12:54 PM, BSO Regional Communications received 'shots fired' radio calls from FLL Deputies and numerous 911 callers. RC immediately enacted Active Shooter/Mass Casualty Protocols

claim: Approximately 90 minutes after the primary FLL shooting, unsubstantiated 'shots fired' reports in Terminal 1 and the Hibiscus Garage triggered a chaotic self-evacuation across the airport that produced additional injuries, with roughly forty people hurt in the rushed evacuation, some suffering broken bones.
source_title: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport Active Shooter Incident and Post-Event Response After Action Report
supporting_excerpt: Approximately 90 minutes after the initial incident, speculation of additional firearms discharged in other areas within FLL caused panic and led to a chaotic self-evacuation of persons throughout the airport ... Almost 40 others were hurt in the rushed evacuation after the attack, with some suffering sprains and bruises and others having broken bones.
caveat: The specific injury count is reported in press aggregations; the AAR characterizes the event as chaotic self-evacuation with substantial secondary injuries.

claim: During the 2013 LAX Terminal 3 shooting, approximately 4,500 passengers self-evacuated from Terminals 1, 2, and 3; more than 20,000 were sheltered in place; the disruption affected roughly 1,500 flights and 171,000 passengers.
source_title: Active Shooter Incident and Resulting Airport Disruption - LAX After Action Report
supporting_excerpt: Approximately 4,500 passengers self-evacuated from Terminals 1, 2, and 3 and more than 20,000 passengers were sheltered in place on aircraft and in terminals. The incident had cascading effects that impacted about 1,500 flights and 171,000 passengers

claim: LAX first operationally deployed the Los Angeles City Wireless Emergency Alert system on airport property during a 2016 false-active-shooter event, in direct response to the 2013 after-action's finding of a communication gap with passengers.
source_title: New Technology, Security Enhancements Critical in Response to False Active-Shooter Reports at LAX
supporting_excerpt: Airport Operations employed for the first time, Los Angeles City's Wireless Emergency Alert (WEA) system at the onset and end of the emergency-response portion of the incident

claim: The FCC adopted rules requiring wireless carriers to deliver device-based location for wireless 911 calls to PSAPs within 30 seconds of call origination as part of location-based routing implementation.
source_title: FCC Fact Sheet - Location-Based Routing for Wireless 911 Calls
supporting_excerpt: For real-time location enabled PSAPs, a caller's location information must be received within 30 seconds from the beginning of a 911 call.
airport_or_entity: US wireless carriers and PSAPs generally
denominator: from origination of 911 call to location delivery
caveat: Implementation deadlines are staged by carrier and by PSAP capability.

claim: NG911 requires PSAPs to receive 911 traffic in IP-based SIP format with location conveyed via PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format - Location Object) or a functional equivalent.
source_title: Next Generation 911 (NG911) - Compliant Emergency Communication
supporting_excerpt: service providers must deliver 911 traffic in an IP-based SIP format with location information embedded in the call signaling using PIDF-LO ... or the functional equivalent.
caveat: Vendor summary; underlying framework is defined by NENA i3 standard and FCC rulings.

claim: IBC Section 907.5.2.1.1 requires audible fire alarm notification appliances to provide a sound pressure level of 15 dBA above the average ambient sound level, or 5 dBA above the maximum sound level having a duration of at least 60 seconds, whichever is greater.
source_title: Fire Alarm System Requirements by Building Type: IBC, IFC, and NFPA 72 Guide
supporting_excerpt: Audible alarm notification appliances must provide a sound pressure level of 15 decibels (dBA) above the average ambient sound level or 5 dBA above the maximum sound level having a duration of not less than 60 seconds, whichever is greater
caveat: Secondary summary; primary text is the IBC, which is paywalled by ICC.

claim: IBC 907.5.2.2 requires an emergency voice/alarm communication (EVAC) system for assembly occupancies with more than 300 occupants, enabling pre-recorded or live voice announcements for orderly evacuation.
source_title: Fire Alarm System Requirements by Building Type: IBC, IFC, and NFPA 72 Guide
supporting_excerpt: For assembly occupancies with more than 300 occupants, an emergency voice/alarm communication (EVAC) system is required per IBC 907.5.2.2, allowing pre-recorded or live voice announcements for orderly evacuation rather than simple horns and strobes.
caveat: Secondary summary; primary IBC text is paywalled.

claim: NFPA 415 provides the airport-specific standard for airport terminal buildings, addressing fire barriers, smoke control for large-volume spaces, egress design for peak occupancy, and evacuation planning for high-rise terminal areas.
source_title: NFPA 415, Standard on Airport Terminal Buildings, Fueling Ramp Drainage, and Loading Walkways
supporting_excerpt: provides requirements for construction and protection of all types of airport terminal buildings, as well as design and maintenance of aircraft fueling ramp drainage and design, construction, and fire protection of loading walkways.
caveat: Underlying standard is paywalled; scope statement is from the NFPA product page.

claim: The ADA requires effective communication so that a person with a vision, hearing, or speech disability can receive information from, and convey information to, the covered entity on an equivalent basis.
source_title: ADA Requirements: Effective Communication
supporting_excerpt: The purpose of the effective communication rules is to ensure that the person with a vision, hearing, or speech disability can communicate with, receive information from, and convey information to, the covered entity.
airport_or_entity: US public accommodations and public entities

claim: ADAAG Section 4.28 provides the technical requirements for visual alarm appliances, including spacing considerations for long corridors typical of shopping malls and airport terminals to minimize composite flash rates.
source_title: ADAAG Manual - Alarms [4.28]
supporting_excerpt: In long corridors, such as in shopping malls and airport terminals, visual alarms should be spaced to minimize their number and the effect of a composite flash rate.

claim: A Labor Day 2019 false alarm at Newark Liberty International Airport caused approximately 150-200 passengers to self-evacuate onto the tarmac after an Alaska Airlines employee triggered an alarm following two men fleeing at Gate 30 in Terminal A.
source_title: False alarm causes panic, fleeing passengers at Newark airport
supporting_excerpt: A false alarm caused panicked Labor Day passengers to flee Newark Liberty International Airport on September 2, 2019, when an Alaska Airlines employee triggered an alarm after two men fled at Gate 30 in Terminal A. The alarm caused about 150 to 200 passengers in the terminal to 'self-evacuate' outside Gate 37.

claim: Airport false-alarm evacuations create material stampede risk because crowd density above approximately four people per square meter is where movement efficiency declines and crowd turbulence begins.
source_title: Airport False Alarms Expose Danger of Panicked Evacuations, Experts Say
supporting_excerpt: Research from the International Journal of Crowd Science highlights that once crowd density exceeds 4 people per square meter, movement efficiency declines, increasing the likelihood of crowd turbulence and stampedes.
denominator: crowd density threshold for movement collapse
caveat: News aggregation citing academic research; original journal reference not verified in this pass.

claim: Terminals are required to provide equivalent visual notification of announcements including gate changes, boarding calls, delays, and emergencies so passengers with hearing impairments receive the same information as hearing passengers.
source_title: Visual alerting device - accessiBe
supporting_excerpt: Terminals are required to broadcast announcements via visual systems, like video monitors, to ensure that no one will miss important announcements. Passengers with hearing impairments receive the same information as hearing passengers - gate changes, boarding calls, delays, and emergencies - through synchronized visual displays.
caveat: Industry reference; underlying requirements derive from ADA effective-communication and Air Carrier Access Act rules.
